newsitem.title: UK: LME copper spreads jump as prices hit 5-month high.
newsitem.headline: LME copper spreads jump as prices hit 5-month high.

text.p: Backwardations flared up during active London Metal Exchange (LME) trading on Tuesday, with December date tightness becoming acute against a background of falling stocks, while the market rose to its highest for five-months.
LME officials monitored the ring trading sessions, which were dominated by business in spreads, largely from the speculative side of the market, traders said.
"It (business) was very active, but orderly," one senior trader said.

There was a twin focus to the spread activity. Nearby dates were sharply higher, with the "tomorrow/next day" rate trading to within $3 of the LME's $23 daily backwardation limit. Cash/one week was at $27 backwardation.
But the sensitive mid-December area was also higher, which resulted in the overall cash/threes backwardation increasing to $220 from $175 on Monday.
"It is all very tight at the moment, and the shorts are looking down a barrel. The thing is, it is genuine physical tightness. There is just not enough metal," one trader said.

Earlier today, the LME reported that copper warehouse stocks had fallen by 3,850 tonnes to just 90,050 tonnes - the lowest for 6-1/4 years. A small tonnage was lifted from Singapore, which allayed recent concerns of larger deliveries being made there.
Three months prices capitalised on the data to hit a high of $2,272 a tonne -- the highest since the Sumitomo Corp scandal erupted in June -- although the attention soon moved towards spreads.

On Monday, the London Clearing House (LCH) doubled the margins required for cash/threes spread positions to $150/tonne, a move some traders said was designed to head off a speculative bandwagon developing in December.

But others said that margins of $150/tonne were still fairly low, given that the initial margin on outright positions was $200. Also the large speculative funds believed to be active in the market at present were financially strong and well able to absorb this.
"I think this (December) tightness) is going to get much worse. There are big shorts out there, and with every rise in cash prices more of those big option strikes come into play," one said.
December 16/18 is where the tightness is concentrated, and this rate rose to $33 backwardation while the premium for December/January increased to $68 from $55 on Monday.

Traders attributed these high premiums to a combination of factors -- rolling foward of some short positions from December 1995, when the LME was also tight, end-year business and covering against yearly options.
Even if stocks started to rise, as was widely expected, the increase of some 20,000/30,000 tonnes would do little to alleviate the picture.
"In reality, these stocks are much lower than people think. Don't forget, when they were last this low the LME did not have warehouses in the U.S. or the Far East," another trader said.
